title.en: The World's Renovation: From the Dew of the Devas to the First Sin
title.zh: 世界重成：天人甘露與初罪

region.en: Abhasvara heaven and the mingled earth-waters (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya, site of the first teaching on this)
region.zh: 光音天與水土相融之初地（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya, vol. v. ff. 155-166, translated c. 8th-9th century); Rockhill's English translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. I, translated from the Dulva (Tibetan Vinaya)

summary.en: When the world was destroyed, its inhabitants were reborn among the Abhasvara (Radiant) devas with ethereal luminous bodies that moved through space and fed on joy; when the merit ran out, they descended to an earth mingled with water and ocean, where a wind solidified the surface like cream on cooling milk, and a rime - the essence of earth, sweet as raw honey - appeared. The beings who tasted it grew coarse, their light went out, and so sun, moon, stars, night, day and the divisions of time were created; and from vanity of complexion and greed for rice came complexion-castes, houses, property, theft, and the election of Mahasammata, the first king.
summary.zh: 世界被毀時，眾生轉生於光音天，身體如光、飛行自在、以喜為食；福報竭時下生於水土相融的大地。風吹其面，如牛乳冷卻時凝結乳皮一般凝成「地味」——色如酥油、味如生蜜。眾生嚐之身粗失光，於是日月星辰、晝夜時分由是而生；因愛美貌起慢、因囤米起貪，種姓、房舍、財產、偷盜次第而現，眾人遂選美大者為「田主」——第一個國王摩訶三末多。

texts.canonical_translation: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha and the early history of his order, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
At the time when the world was destroyed, many of its inhabitants were born in the region of the Abhasvara devas, and there they had ethereal bodies, free from every impurity; light proceeded from their persons, they moved through space and fed on joy, and they lived to great ages. In the meanwhile the great earth was mingled up with the waters and with the mighty deep, and over the face of this mixture blew a wind which solidified and concentrated the rich surface, as wind blowing over boiled milk cooling solidifies the cream; this rime, the essence of the earth, was of exquisite colour, delicious taste and delightful fragrance, in colour like butter and in taste like uncooked honey. When the allotted time of some of the radiant beings was accomplished, they departed that life and became men with attributes similar to those they had before. At that period there was neither sun nor moon, no stars, no night or day, no minutes, seconds, months, periods of time or years; neither were there males or females - there were only animated beings.

Then a being of an inquisitive nature tasted the rime with the tip of his finger and conceived a liking for it, and began to eat pieces of it as food; others followed his example, and from eating it their bodies became coarse and gross, they lost their brilliancy, and darkness was upon the face of the earth. For these reasons the sun and moon were created, and stars, night and day, minutes, seconds, months, half-months and years. The beings who ate little of the food kept a clear complexion, and those who ate much grew dark; the clear-complexioned boasted and became sinful and iniquitous, and so distinctions were established - and then the rime vanished. In its place appeared a fatty substance, then bunches of reeds of exquisite colour and flavour, each vanishing in turn when pride and greed returned; and finally a spontaneously growing rice, clean, huskless, four fingers long, that if cut down in the evening was grown again by morning.

From eating this rice their different organs were developed - some had those of males and others those of females - and conceiving love for each other they came to commit fornication. Other beings, seeing what they were doing, threw at them earth, stones, gravel, pebbles and potsherds, crying 'thou doest wrongly!' - exactly as, nowadays, when a man takes unto himself a wife, her friends sprinkle her with dust, perfumes, flowers and parched rice crying 'good luck, sister!' And thus what was formerly considered unlawful has become lawful, what was not tolerated is tolerated, what was looked down on has become praiseworthy. Possessed by wickedness, the sinful beings commenced building houses - 'here,' they said, 'we may do what is not allowed' - and from this expression originated the word 'house', the first division by houses in the world, lawful or not lawful according to the king's decision.

Then an indolent being took at one time enough rice for evening and morning, another enough for two, three, seven days, another for a fortnight and a month - and because they laid up provisions, the spontaneously growing rice became coarse, a husk enveloped the grain, and when it had been cut down it grew no more. Assembling in sorrow and lamentation, they drew lines of demarcation and established boundaries - this is thine, this is mine - and when one person took another's rice without consent and refused to mend his ways, they chose from their midst the finest-looking, largest, handsomest and strongest, and made him lord over their fields: he should punish the punishable and recompense the praiseworthy, and receive a portion of the produce. From his receiving the homage of many he was called Mahasammata; as protector of the fields he was called Kshatriya; and as a righteous, wise man who brought happiness to mankind with the law, he was called Raja. From those who went to the wilds with diseases came the Brahmans of meditation and mantra; from the handicraft-sellers came the Vaisyas; and members of all castes who cut off their hair and put on saffron robes made the fourth caste, that of the Sramanas - while from the first theft, sin now exists in the world in which there had been no trace of it.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the Tibetan Dulva's account of the renovation is the corpus's cosmogony of the current world-epoch (bhadrakalpa); it grounds both the creation of time itself and the social order in one causal chain of appetite - sin appears in the world not as a fall but as a series of firsts, each one 'lawful or not lawful according to the king's decision.'

functions: Cosmogonic doctrine of the Buddha's own teaching lineage: the current world-epoch arises from radiant beings who descend by exhausted merit
Founding charters of time, sex, property, house, kingship and caste as a single chain of 'firsts' caused by appetite
Explains the wedding sprinkling-custom as the survival of the primordial stoning of the first sinners
Taught by the Buddha (or by Maudgalyayana at his request) to show the bhikshus how sin first appeared in the world

variants.name: Agganna Sutta of the Digha Nikaya
variants.summary: The Pali parallel has the Buddha fear the tirthikas would accuse him of extolling his own clan and has Maudgalyayana tell the story to the Shakyas; the Tibetan Dulva third-volume recension follows this, while the fifth-volume version is told by the Buddha himself to the bhikshus.

variants.name: Abhasvara devas in the Northern (Sanskrit-Tibetan) recension
variants.summary: The Tibetan text names the radiant heaven Abhasvara and dwells on the wind-cream simile and the rime as 'essence of the earth' (prithivirasa), details abbreviated in the Pali parallel.

sensitivity.note: Canonical Buddhist narrative of living tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation only. Motif tags are interpretive: the 'clay-humans' tag is only an analogy to world-parents molding humans, noted here because the Tibetan text has humans condensing from a food-substance rather than being molded.

A fatty substance appeared next, then bunches of reeds, each vanishing in turn; finally a spontaneously growing rice, clean and four fingers long, which if cut in the evening was grown again by morning.

And thus what was formerly unlawful has become lawful, what was looked down on has become praiseworthy. The sinful built houses to do what was not allowed, hoarded rice until the spontaneous crop turned husky, drew boundary lines - this is thine, this is mine - and when theft appeared chose the finest, largest and strongest among them as lord of the fields: Mahasammata, protector of the fields, the righteous king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Impaled Rishi and the Sun-Family of the Shakyas

region.en: Potala and the hermitage of Krichnavarna (symbolic pin at Potala hill)
region.zh: 補怛洛迦山與黑衣仙人之淨修林（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya vol. iii. ff. 420-439), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. I, translated from the Dulva

summary.en: King Karnika's virtuous son Gautama takes vows under the rishi Krichnavarna while his wicked brother rules; a murdered courtesan's sword is found in his hut, and he is impaled outside the southern gate. His master's truth-asseveration turns Krichnavarna golden (Kanakavarna), and by a great rain and a mighty wind two drops of Gautama's mingled semen and blood fall as eggs; the sun's heat hatches two children in a sugar-cane plantation - born of the rising sun, hence the Solar race, born of Gautama, hence Gautama, found in sugar-cane, hence Ikshvaku - the dynasty of the Buddha.
summary.zh: 補怛洛迦王賢德長子喬達摩出家於黑衣仙人；妓女被害，兇手將血劍棄於其茅舍，眾人以為兇犯，將他活釘於南門外。仙人以其「無罪之誓」由黑轉金，又降大雨起狂風撫其痛楚，兩滴精血落地成卵，日光孵出兩童於甘蔗園中——因日出而生稱日族、因喬達摩所生稱喬達摩種、因拾於蔗園稱甘蔗王族：此即佛陀之家世。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative of living tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Gautama, though the elder son, begged his father to allow him to become a recluse, dreading the responsibility of a sovereign ruler; a courtesan of Potala called Bhadra was killed by her crafty lover near the recluse's hut, into which the murderer threw his bloody sword, and the people, finding the murdered woman and the sword in the hermit's hut, condemned him to death. He was marched through the city in rags with a wreath of karapira flowers around his neck, taken outside the southern gate, and impaled while yet alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: His master Krichnavarna questioned him as to his guilt; if I am innocent, said Gautama, may you from black become golden-coloured! - and straightway the rishi became golden-coloured, known thereafter as Kanakavarna. Worried that the throne of Potala would become vacant, the rishi caused a great rain to fall on Gautama and a mighty wind to soothe his pains, and two drops of semen mingled with blood fell from him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two drops became eggs, and the heat of the rising sun caused them to open, and two children came out and went into a sugar-cane plantation near by; as the sun's heat went on increasing the rishi Gautama dried up and died. Having been born as the sun arose, the children were called of the sun family, Suryavansa; being the children of Gautama, Gautama; born from his loins, Angirasas; and having been found in a sugar-cane plantation, Ikshvaku. The elder died without issue and the younger became king under the name of Ikshvaku; a hundred of his descendants reigned in Potala, and of their line came the Shakyas and the Buddha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Exiled Princes and the Founding of Kapilavastu
title.zh: 四子被逐與迦毘羅衛建城

region.en: Hermitage of the rishi Kapila on the Bhagirathi (symbolic pin at Kapilvastu, Nepal)
region.zh: 恆伽提河畔迦毘仙人淨修林（以尼泊爾迦毘羅衛為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. I, translated from the Dulva

summary.en: King Virudhaka of the Ikshvaku line, bound by a marriage-bargain to crown his youngest son, exiles his four elder sons with their sisters; at the hermitage of the rishi Kapila they take wives of a different mother - to keep the race from dying out - and build a town the rishi marks out with golden sand, named Kapilavastu for the soil he gave. When Virudhaka hears of his comely sons, he exclaims 'the daring young men!' - and daring they remain: the Shakyas.
summary.zh: 甘蔗王族之主受母家脅迫立幼子為儲，將四個英武王子連同姊妹放逐；他們至迦毘仙人淨修林，聽仙人言娶異母之姊妹為妻以延血統，並依仙人指點以金砂和水畫界建城，因得仙人賜土而名迦毘羅衛。老國王聞悉諸子作為，驚呼「好大膽的年輕人！」——「釋迦」（能仁、勇者）之名由此而得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; the sister-marriage belongs to the traditional genealogy, reported factually.

passages.text: Virudhaka married a second time on condition that if his wife bore a son he should be king; when the child had grown up, the king, on the representation of his wife's father, was obliged to declare his youngest son successor and exile his four other sons. The princes set out with their sisters and a great many people, travelled toward the Himalaya, and coming to the hermitage of the rishi Kapila on the bank of the Bhagirathi, built huts of leaves and fed on the produce of their hunting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Following the rishi's advice they took as wives sisters who were not of the same mother as themselves, and so had many children; the rishi marked out the town-site with golden sand mixed with water, and having given the soil of the place they called it the soil of Kapila, Kapilavastu. Later a deva pointed out another spot, where they built the town of Devadaha, and they made a law in general assembly that they should marry only one wife, and she of their own clan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Virudhaka thought one day of his comely sons and heard their adventures, he exclaimed 'the daring young men! the daring young men!' - and from this they became known as Shakyas. His descendants, fifty-five thousand in number, reigned in Kapilavastu down to Sinhahanu, whose sons were Shuddhodana and the uncles of the Blessed One.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Birth of the Bodhisattva in the Lumbini Grove

region.en: Lumbini grove near Kapilavastu (symbolic pin at Lumbini, Nepal)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛附近的藍毘尼園（以尼泊爾藍毘尼為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya vol. iii. f. 446ff.), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II, translated from the Dulva

summary.en: The future Buddha in the Tushita heaven makes the five preliminary examinations - family, country, time, race and woman - and enters Mahamaya's womb at midnight in the appearance of an elephant; she dreams of a six-tusked white elephant, of moving in space, of ascending a rocky mountain, of a multitude bowing down. Caught by labour in the Lumbini garden she seizes an ashoka tree while Shataketu (Indra) disperses the crowd, and the Bodhisattva takes seven steps to each of the cardinal points with a vow for each direction - then washings of cold and warm water fall on his head. On the same day the future kings Prasenajit, Bimbisara, Udayana and Pradyota are born with the world lit up, and at the temple the yaksha Shakyavardana bows at the child's feet: he is named All-fulfilled, Mighty One of the Shakyas, and God of gods.
summary.zh: 未來佛在兜率天作五觀察——族、地、時、種、女——於半夜化作白象入摩耶夫人胎中；夫人夢六牙白象入胎、凌空飛行、登上大山、眾人禮拜。藍毘尼園中臨盆，手攀無憂樹；帝釋化老嫗欲接聖嬰，被嬰遣回，隨即向四方各行七步，各發一願——「我將至最勝涅槃」「我將為一切眾生之首」「此為我最後之生」「我將渡生死之海」——頭上落下冷熱二水洗浴，誕生處湧出浴母之泉。同日世間四位未來國王誕生，而神殿中的夜叉像竟向嬰兒頂禮：得名「一切義成」「釋迦牟尼」「天人中尊」。

texts.canonical_translation: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha, London 1884 (public domain)

narrative.en:
During King Sinhahanu's reign the Shakya country enjoyed peace; the future Buddha was in the Tushita heaven, and knowing that his time had come, made the five preliminary examinations - of the proper family, of the country, of the time, of the race, and of the woman - and having decided that Mahamayi was the right mother, in the midnight watch entered her womb under the appearance of an elephant. Then the queen had four dreams: she saw a six-tusked white elephant enter her womb, she moved in space above, she ascended a great rocky mountain, and a great multitude bowed down to her. The soothsayers predicted that she would bring forth a son with the thirty-two signs of the great man - if he stays at home he will become a universal monarch; but if he shaves his hair and beard and leaves his home for a homeless state, he will become a Tathagata, an arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.

While visiting the Lumbini garden the pains of childbirth came upon her, and she seized hold of a wide-spreading ashoka tree. Then Shataketu - Indra - caused a violent rain to fall and a wind to blow that dispersed all the crowd of attendants, and assuming the appearance of an old woman went to receive the new-born child in his lap; but the Bodhisattva ordered him back, and took seven steps in the direction of each of the cardinal points. Looking to the east he said, 'I will reach the highest nirvana'; to the south, 'I will be the first of all creatures'; to the west, 'This will be my last birth'; to the north, 'I will cross the ocean of existence.' In accordance with what happens at the birth of every Buddha there fell on his head a stream of cold water and one of warm which washed him, and at the spot where he had been born there appeared a spring in which his mother bathed.

On the same day as the Buddha's birth, kings' sons were born with the world illuminated: Prasenajit of Shravasti, Bimbisara the son of queen Bimbi in Rajagriha, Udayana of Kaushambi, and Pradyota of Ujjayani. Many blessings came to the child's father, so the child was called Sarvarthasiddha, All-fulfilled; and as the Shakyas' custom was to make new-born children bow at the feet of the yaksha Shakyavardana, the king took the child to the temple - but the yaksha bowed down at his feet. On the way every one was struck with the infant's bold appearance, so he received the name of Shakyamuni, the mighty one of the Shakyas; and when the king saw the yaksha bow he exclaimed, 'he is the god of gods!', so the child was called Devatideva.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the Tibetan Dulva nativity grounds the Buddha's birth in the same narrative economy as the four kings born the same day; the seven steps and four vows compress the whole career - nirvana, sovereignty, finality, crossing - into the infant's first movements.

functions: Nativity doctrine: the Bodhisattva chooses his mother by five examinations, so the birth is planned merit, not accident
The four cardinal vows compress the Buddha's whole future ministry into the seven steps of the new-born
Links the Buddha's birth-day with the birthdays of four royal patrons-to-be, the earthly framework of his later ministry
The temple-yaksha's bow transfers sacred authority from the old cult image to the child

variants.name: Lalita Vistara recension
variants.summary: The Lalita Vistara has seven steps east and seven west rather than the four-direction scheme of the Dulva, and develops the nativity pageantry at greater length; Rockhill notes the disagreement.

variants.name: Southern (Pali) nativity
variants.summary: The Pali account agrees on the dream and the steps but makes the bathing by two streams the devas' act and names the birth-tree plainly; the Tibetan text's detail of Indra disguised as an old woman receiving the child is distinctive.

title.en: The Seer Asita and the Word Passed to Katyayana

region.en: Sarvadhara mountain hermitage (symbolic pin at Kapilvastu)
region.zh: 一切護山仙人住處（以迦毘羅衛為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: The mighty seer Asita of the Sarvadhara mountain comes with his nephew Nalada to see the new-born, takes him in his arms, and prophesies: at twenty-nine he will leave home, be an ascetic six years, then find the drink of the cessation of death. Dying soon after, Asita begs Nalada to join the young Shakya's order when the truth is found; Nalada studies mantras among five hundred Brahmans and, converted later by the Buddha, becomes Mahakatyayana, 'the great member of Katya's family.'
summary.zh: 一切護山的大仙人阿私陀偕姪那羅陀探望新生兒，抱之於懷而預言：二十九歲出家、苦行六年、得「不死之甘露」。臨終前囑咐姪兒待其證道後加入釋迦教團；那羅陀於五百梵志中學咒，後為佛陀所化，號大迦旃延。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The two came to see the child, and Asita took him in his arms and asked what had been prophesied about him. He predicted that he would leave his home at twenty-nine, that he would be an ascetic for six years, and that then he would find the drink of the cessation of death. Shortly after, feeling his end approaching, he begged Nalada to enter the order of the young Shakya as soon as he should have found the truth, and then he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nalada went to Varanasi and entered a company of five hundred mantra-studying Brahmans, and as he was of the family of Katya he became known as Katyayana; later on, having been converted by the Buddha, he was called Mahakatyayana, the great member of Katya's family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Devadatta's Elephant and the Bodhisattva's Throw
title.zh: 提婆達多殺象與菩薩擲象

region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城外大道（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: The Licchavis of Vaisali send the Bodhisattva a magnificently jewelled elephant - and the envious Devadatta kills it with a blow of his fist; Nanda drags it aside, and the Bodhisattva, catching it by the tail, throws it over seven fences and ditches so hard it digs the 'elephant ditch', Hastigarta, where believers build a stupa. In the archery contest his arrow pierces every target and drives so deep into the ground it springs a well - and there too the faithful build a stupa.
summary.zh: 吠舍離離車族獻上寶飾大象；嫉妒的提婆達多一拳將象擊斃。難陀將屍體拖至路旁，菩薩抓住象尾擲過七重牆溝，落地成坑——「象坑」（虎多迦多）即由此得名，信眾於此建塔。比箭時菩薩之箭貫穿全部箭靶、深入土中湧出清泉，信眾又於彼處建塔。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: When they were near the town Devadatta noticed the jewelled elephant, and, filled with envy, killed it with a blow of his fist; Nanda, coming that way, threw the carcass to one side, but the Bodhisattva, taking it by the tail, threw it over seven fences and ditches, and it dug a great ditch in falling which became known as the elephant ditch, Hastigarta - and there the believing Brahmans and householders built a stupa which is reverenced to the present day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: And here it is said: Devadatta killed the mighty elephant, Nanda carried it seven paces, the Bodhisattva through space with his hand did cast it as a stone far away. After this the young Shakyas tried their skill at archery; the arrow of the Bodhisattva, after piercing all the targets, went so far into the ground that it caused a spring to rush forth - and there also the believers built a stupa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Goose and the Arrow: Devadatta's First Quarrel
title.zh: 雁與箭：提婆達多結怨之始

region.en: Gardens on the banks of the Rohita river (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 羅希塔河畔林園（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Summoned to free the great tree blocking Kapilavastu's water, the prince is first tested in the gardens by Devadatta shooting a goose overhead; it falls in the Bodhisattva's garden, who extracts the arrow and binds the wound - and refuses to give up the bird: it belongs not to him who attempted to take its life, but to him who saved it. This was the first quarrel between the two.
summary.zh: 菩薩應召為城民移除堵水的大樹；途經園林，提婆達多一箭射落天上飛雁，雁落入菩薩園中。菩薩為其拔箭裹傷，並拒絕交出：雁屬於救其命者，不屬於欲害其命者——二人結怨由此而始。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: While they were still in the gardens Devadatta saw a goose flying overhead, so he shot it, and it fell in the Bodhisattva's garden; he took it, extracted the arrow and bound up its wound. Devadatta sent a messenger to claim the bird, but the Bodhisattva would not give it up, saying that it belonged not to him who had attempted to take its life, but to him who had saved it - and this was the first quarrel between these two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Encounters on the Road

region.en: Parks and roads of Kapilavastu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城內園林道路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Driving in the park, the prince sees an old man, and the charioteer Chhandaka must explain what old age is - all are subject to it; a dropsical, emaciated man teaches him disease; a torch-lit litter of many-coloured stuffs with wailing, dishevelled women is a corpse, and to this state all must come; and a deva of the pure abode, appearing as a shaven mendicant with an alms-bowl, shows him the man who has forsaken the world. Each time the prince turns back home pensively.
summary.zh: 太子出遊園林：先見老人，御者闡陀只能講明何為老——「無人能免」；再見浮腫枯瘦之病人，得知何為病；又遇火把簇擁的彩轎與披髮哀哭的婦女——那是屍體，「人人終將如此」；最後遇見化為剃度乞士的淨居天子，知世間另有「捨離在家」之人。太子每見一景，皆鬱鬱回宮。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: In the park he saw an old man, and the charioteer explained what old age was and how all were subject to it; deeply impressed, the prince turned back and went home. A short time after, out driving, he met a dropsical man, emaciated and weak, with faculties impaired, and Chhandaka told him what disease was - and again he turned back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another time he came across a procession bearing along on a litter, with burning torches, something wrapped in many-coloured stuffs, the women accompanying it with dishevelled hair crying piteously: it was a corpse, Chhandaka told him, and to this state all must come. And yet on another occasion he met a deva of the pure abode who had assumed the appearance of a shaved and shorn mendicant bearing an alms-bowl, going from door to door - one who has forsaken the world, a righteous, virtuous man. Then pensively he drove back to the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ploughmen and the Immovable Shade

region.en: Ploughed fields of a village near Kapilavastu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛近郊田疇（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Sent to divert himself watching the ploughmen, the prince finds the labourers hair erect, covered with sweat, and the oxen pricked with iron goads, bleeding at the mouth and nose, covered with gadflies. His tender heart freed them all - 'from today you are no longer slaves; go where you please and live in joy' - and the oxen to the sweetest grass and purest water; then, seated in meditation under a jambu-tree, he was found by his father, and lo! the shade had not moved from where he was.
summary.zh: 國王令太子散心觀耕；他見農夫汗流浹背、耕牛遭鐵刺傷口流血、蠅虻蔽體，大發悲心，當即釋放眾人「從今日起你們不再是奴隸」，牛亦得甘草淨水。隨後他在一株閻浮樹下入定沉思，父親尋來時——樹影竟然不移，始終覆在其身。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: He saw the labourers with hair erect, uncovered hands and feet, their bodies dirty and running with sweat, and the work-oxen pricked with iron goads, their backs streaming with blood, covered with gadflies and mosquitoes, the ploughshare wounding them. His tender heart was touched with compassion: to whom do you belong? - we are the king's property. From to-day you are no longer slaves; you shall be no longer servants; go where you please and live in joy. He freed also the oxen: from to-day eat the sweetest grass and drink the purest water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, seeing a shady jambu-tree on one side, he sat down at its foot and gave himself to earnest meditation; and there his father found him - and lo! the shade had not moved from where he was. Through the lengthening afternoon the tree had kept its shelter over the absorbed prince as faithfully as an attendant, and the king, coming up at the edge of the furrows where the oxen had been freed that same day, stood silent before the unmoving shadow before he dared to wake his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.zh: 喬波之贊與鹿女郎之偈

region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城頭（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Riding home from freeing the great tree, the prince is seen from her terrace by Gopa, daughter of the Shakya Kinkinisvara - they stop and gaze - and the king makes her his son's wife. Later, returning from the Rajagriha cemetery, he is met by Mrigadja's song from her window - 'happy is his mother, happy his father, happy she whose husband he shall be, that woman has gone beyond sorrow!' - and he throws her a necklace for her pretty words; the king hears of it and weds her too, seven days before the flight from home, with Yaśodhara and 60,000 attendant women.
summary.zh: 太子移樹歸城，麒麟獅王之女喬波自露臺見之，二人相視出神，國王遂以其為子媳。其後菩薩自王舍城屍林回城，鹿女郎（彌迦闍）自窗中唱偈：「其母有福！其父有福！將為其妻者，已出離憂苦！」菩薩擲一寶鏈酬其妙語；國王聞之又娶之為妃。故其妻有耶輸陀羅、喬波、鹿女等，侍女六萬，而鹿女入門僅七日，他便離家而去。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Gopa saw him from the terrace of her house as he was riding home, and he also noticing her stopped his chariot to look at her; the people saw that they were fascinated with each other and told the king, who took Gopa and made her his son's wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: As he was going back to the city Mrigadja, the daughter of the Shakya Kalika, saw him from her window and sang: ah! happy is his mother; his father also, happy is he; ah! she whose husband he shall be, that woman has gone beyond sorrow! The Bodhisattva threw her a necklace to pay her for her pretty words, and the king, hearing of it, made her the Bodhisattva's wife - so his wives were Gopa, Mrigadja and 60,000 attendant women, and Mrigadja became his wife seven days before he left his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

region.en: Eastern gate of Kapilavastu and the night road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛東門與夜路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Guarded at four gates by his uncles, the Bodhisattva passes the night amid a sleeping harem that looks like the dead; Yaśodhara dreams he is abandoning her and asks to go wherever he goes. Indra and the gods exhort him; Chhandaka saddles Kanthaka, and the devatas of the palace weep like rain. At the eastern gate he greets his sleeping father - 'though I love thee, I must free myself from the fear of age and death' - passes Mahanaman's begging patrol, rides twelve yojanas, and sends his horse and charioteer home; his cut hair is carried by Shataketu to the Trayastrimcat heaven, and an old woman's legacy robe - the cotton garment of ten Pratyeka Buddhas - is exchanged with a hunter who is Indra in disguise.
summary.zh: 四門皆有叔父重兵把守；王宮後宮熟睡如死人，令菩薩心生厭離。耶輸陀羅夢他離去，求同行。帝釋率諸天相勸，闡陀備好神駒犍陟，宮中天人淚如雨下。東門外他向熟睡的父親告別：「我雖愛父，但須解脫老病死之怖。」又避開巡夜的難陀，一夜行十二由旬，隨即打髮馬與御者回城；剪下的頭髮被帝釋送往三十三天；又以「十辟支佛相傳、囑轉贈佛陀」之棉衣，換取帝釋所扮老獵人身上的粗衣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: On the night of the seventh day the Bodhisattva noticed all his sleeping harem, and the women looked so like the dead in their sleep that he was filled with loathing; on the same night Yaśodhara dreamt he was abandoning her, and awoke and told her lord of her dream: where'er thou goest, there let me go to. Cataketu (Indra) and the other gods came and exhorted him to flee the world, and told Chhandaka to saddle the treasure-horse Kanthaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The devatas inhabiting the palace commenced to cry, so that their tears fell like rain; at the eastern gate he perceived his sleeping father and cried, father, though I love thee, yet a fear possesses me and I may not stay - I must free myself from the fear of conquering time and death, of the horrors of age and death! Suddenly he came across Mahanaman patrolling the city, and though his cousin begged and cried aloud, telling him of all the sorrow he was bringing, he travelled that night twelve yojanas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: He stopped and told Chhandaka to return to the city with the horse and the jewels; the prince took his sword and cut off his hair, which he threw into the air, and Shataketu took it and carried it off to the Trayastrimcat heaven - there the faithful built the stupa of the taking of the hair and beard. Then, as a decrepit hunter wearing the cotton garment handed down through ten Pratyeka Buddhas for the son of Shuddhodana, Shataketu exchanged clothes with him, and the Bodhisattva went on to Rajagriha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Bimbisara's Offer on the Pandava Mountain
title.zh: 頻毘娑羅王靈鷲山相會

region.en: Pandava mountain near Rajagriha (symbolic pin at Gridhakuta)
region.zh: 王舍城外靈鷲山（以耆闍崛山為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Bimbisara, seeing the ascetic's noble bearing from his palace terrace, fills his bowl and follows him to the Pandava mountain, offering everything that makes life agreeable - women, riches, pleasures. The ascetic answers with the great renunciation-verses: the treasure I am seeking is that wisdom which knoweth no superior; and the king, 'when thou shalt have reached thy goal, teach it then to me,' receives the promise.
summary.zh: 頻毘娑羅王自宮中望見乞士風儀，令人布施、令人隨行，親登靈鷲山以財色諸樂相許。行者答曰：我屬釋迦日族，不慕世財；「我所求者，是無上智慧」；王曰「汝證道時，願以斯法教我」——王子允諾。此為日後王舍城弘法之伏筆。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Bimbisara noticed the ascetic from the terrace of his palace, was struck with his noble bearing, sent some one to fill his bowl and another to see where he went; then he went to visit him on the Pandava mountain and offered him everything that makes life agreeable - women, riches and pleasures. I care not for this world's treasures; they cannot bring contentment, the ascetic answered, 'tis hard to cross the swamps of human passions - the treasure I am seeking is that wisdom which knoweth no superior. When thou shalt have reached thy goal, teach it then to me, said the king, and the Bodhisattva promised that he would.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

region.en: Bank of the Nairanjana river at Gaya (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 恒河南岸尼連禪河畔（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Surpassing all the ascetics of the Vulture's Peak, the Bodhisattva learns their goal is only Sakra-hood and moves on; refusing the gods' offer of miraculous feeding, he fasts to a single pea a day until his body is emaciated and blackish-red. Yaśodhara, hearing the reports, puts away her flowers and jewels and copies his mortifications until her father-in-law forbids anyone to speak of him. Seeing severe asceticism had not brought him nearer the truth, he takes food of an unpalatable kind and sleeps beside a corpse in the cemetery - where village girls throw dirt and stones at him, thinking him a flesh-eating fiend; his five attendants forsake him for Benares, where they become 'the Five.'
summary.zh: 他在靈鷲山苦行勝過一切仙人，知其所求不過帝釋之位，遂離去；諸天願以神力供養，他亦拒絕，日食一豆，身瘦如柴、色如黑紅。耶輸陀羅聞訊，棄珠花而同修苦行，直至公公下令不得再提其名。菩薩知苦行無益，食粗糲之物，臥屍林屍旁而眠——村女誤為啖人羅剎，投以泥土瓦礫；五侍者失望而去，往波羅奈鹿野苑，是為「五比丘」。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: He lived with the ascetics of the Vulture's Peak, surpassing them all in his mortifications, so that he became known as the great ascetic; but he finally learned from them that the object they had in view was to become Sakra or Brahma or even Mara, and knew that they were not in the right way. The gods offered to feed him miraculously and unknown to mankind, but he refused, and went on fasting until he reduced his food to a single pea a day, and his body was emaciated and of a blackish-red colour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yaśodhara, greatly grieved, put away her flowers and jewels and performed the same mortifications which her husband was practising, until Shuddhodana, fearing for the child she bore, forbade any one to speak to her about the Bodhisattva. When he had obtained and eaten some very unpalatable food he wandered into the cemetery, and lying down beside a corpse went to sleep; the village girls saw him and thought he was a fiend seeking human flesh to devour, and threw dirt and stones at him - and his five attendants, forsaking him, started out for Benares and dwelt in the Mrigadava as the Five.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Milk-Soup of Nanda and Nandabala
title.zh: 難陀與難陀波羅的乳糜

region.en: Village of Senani near the Nairanjana (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 尼連禪河畔舍那村（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: The headman's daughters Nanda and Nandabala, hearing of the Shakya prince foretold to be chakravartin or Buddha, prepare milk-soup for him; he takes it in a crystal vase brought by two devas of the Akanishta region, bathes in the Nairanjana, is handed out by an arjuna branch the devas bend down, and eats on the bank. His washed bowl, thrown into the river, is seized by the Nagas - until Shakra, as a garuda, dives and carries it to the Trayastrimcat heaven, where the gods build the stupa of the bowl. Asked what they seek by their gift, the sisters answer they wish to become his wives at his chakravartin rebirth - and he explains that could never be.
summary.zh: 舍那村長的兩個女兒難陀與難陀波羅聽聞釋迦太子將為轉輪王或佛陀，預備乳糜供養；他以光音天（阿迦膩吒天）二天子送來的水晶缽受食，入河沐浴——諸天彎下阿順那樹枝助其出水。飯畢洗缽擲於河中，龍王取之；帝釋化身大鵬入水奪缽，帶往三十三天建「缽塔」。二女問供養何求，答曰願其成轉輪王時為其妻；他為之解說此願不可得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Nanda and Nandabala had heard about the Shakya prince of the Kapilavastu Shakyas, and that it had been prophesied of him that he would become a universal monarch or a Buddha; so they had prepared for him a milk-soup, which the Bodhisattva took in a crystal vase adorned with jewels which two devas of the Akanishta region had brought him. Carrying the food with him he went to the Nairanjana river and bathed, and when he had finished the devas bent down the branches of an arjuna tree, which he seized to help him out of the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having washed the bowl, he threw it into the river; the Nagas took it, but Shakra, assuming the form of a garuda, dashed into the river, seized the bowl and carried it off to the Trayastrimcat heaven, and there the gods built the stupa of the bowl. Asked what they sought by their gift, the sisters answered that the soothsayers had prophesied he would become a chakravartin monarch - may this seed of virtue make you become our husband at that time; he explained that this could never be, and they said, may you then quickly reach the highest wisdom and perfection.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Mara's Defeat at the Bodhi Tree

region.en: Bodhi tree at Uruvilva (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 閻浮提菩提樹下（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Wading the river amid wondrous signs, the Bodhisattva takes from the grass-merchant Svastika - Shakra in disguise - a handful of grass for his seat under the Bodhi tree. Mara comes with the lie that Devadatta has crushed the Shakyas and apparitions of his wives and kinsmen, argues, sends his three daughters Desire, Pleasure and Delight with all their allurements - and the Bodhisattva changes them into old hags. The gods of the pure abode shower flowers on the conqueror and sing victory; reasoning within himself he sees the chain of causes and effects that brings existence, age and death - and becomes enlightened. Mara's bow and standard fall from his grasp, and a million and thirty-six thousand cohorts flee filled with dismay.
summary.zh: 菩薩涉河時異象頻現；帝釋化身賣草人婆藪陀，獻一把草為菩提樹下之座。魔王先以「提婆達多滅釋迦族」之謊、再以耶輸陀羅等親眷幻影、繼以雄辯、最後遣三女「欲、樂、喜」百般誘惑——菩薩不動，反令三女化為老嫗。淨居諸天雨花唱勝；菩薩於座上思維，徹見生死流轉之緣起，遂成正覺。魔王弓箭旗幟墜地，百萬三千六百魔軍驚惶潰散。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Shakra took the shape of the grass merchant Svastika, and from him the Bodhisattva obtained a handful of grass out of which he made his seat at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Then Mara went to him and said, Devadatta has subdued Kapilavastu; he has seized the palace and crushed the Shakyas - why stay you here? He caused apparitions of Yaśodhara, of Mrigadja, of Gopa, of Devadatta and of the Shakyas who had escaped to appear before him, but the Bodhisattva remained unmoved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Mara called his three daughters, Desire, Pleasure and Delight, and they tried all their allurements in vain; the Bodhisattva changed them into old hags. Seeing all his devices fail, the gods of the pure abode showered down flowers on the conqueror and sang songs of victory; and reasoning within himself the Bodhisattva saw the cause of existence, of age, of death, and the way to free oneself of all this trouble - the concatenation of causes and effects which bring about existence and its cessation became known to him, and he became enlightened, a Buddha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: When all wisdom had been given him, Mara's bow and his standard fell from his grasp, and all his cohorts, a million and thirty-six thousand in number, fled filled with dismay. The rumour had reached Kapilavastu that the prince had died under the excess of his penances and all the court was in despair; then came the news that he had attained enlightenment, and great was the rejoicing everywhere.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

region.zh: 迦毘羅衛池畔（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: On the day the enlightenment-news reaches Kapilavastu, Yaśodhara bears a son - and Rahu seizes the moon, so the eclipse marks the child: Rahula. The same day Amritodana's wife bears a son amid the city's rejoicing: All-joy, Ananda. But Shuddhodana doubts the child is his son's, and the mother, in great distress, sets the child on a stone and sinks both in the water: if the child be the Bodhisattva's, may it and the stone float! - and lo, it floats like a ball of cotton, and the people rejoice and take the young child out of the pond.
summary.zh: 證道之訊抵迦毘羅衛之日，耶輸陀羅產下一子；而當日「羅睺」蝕月，故子名羅睺羅。同日阿彌多陀那之妻亦生子，城中方大慶，遂名「一切喜」——阿難。淨飯王疑此子非其孫，母親大慟，將孩子置於石上同沉水中發願：「若真是菩薩之子，願子與石俱浮！」果然嬰兒浮於石上如棉團，眾人大喜，將孩子抱出。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Just as the king was being told the news of the enlightenment, they came and told him that Yaśodhara had brought forth a son, and also that Rahu had seized the moon; so they called the child Rahula. On the same day the wife of Amritodana brought forth a son, and as the city was rejoicing greatly that day, they called him All-joy, Ananda.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Shuddhodana thought that Yaśodhara's child could not be Shakyamuni's, and great was the mother's distress on hearing his suspicions; so she took the child to a pond, put it on a stone, and placed them together in the water with these words: if the child be the Bodhisattva's, may it and the stone float; if it is not, may it sink! And lo! the child floated on the stone as if it had been a ball of cotton, and the people rejoiced greatly and took the young child out of the pond.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Offering: Trapusha and Bhallika

region.en: Bank of the Nairanjana under the Bo tree (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 菩提樹下尼連禪河畔（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: Seven days after enlightenment two merchants, Trapusha and Bhallika, with five hundred waggons are led by a deva to offer honey-sweetened food; each of the four great kings of the cardinal points brings a bowl, and not wishing to offend any of them the Buddha takes the four and transforms them into one. He bids them go for refuge to the Buddha, the truth and the church that will hereafter exist - the first lay disciples - and whatever wish they made will be granted.
summary.zh: 證道七日後，商人提謂與波利率五百車隊，蒙天人指引獻上蜜和之食；四方四大天王各捧一缽前來，佛不欲偏捨，合四缽為一缽受之，並教二人皈依佛、法與「將來之僧」——是為最早的在家二弟子，且許諾「汝等所願皆得成就」。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: When the seven days were passed there came along two merchants, Trapusha and Bhallika, with five hundred waggons; and following the advice of a deva they came to the Buddha and offered him food sweetened with honey. Each of the four great kings of the cardinal points brought him a bowl in which to take the food, and not wishing to offend any of them he took the four bowls and transformed them into one. Then the Buddha said to the merchants, go for a refuge to the Buddha, to the truth and to the church that will hereafter exist; whatever wish you may have made when you made me this offering, it will be granted unto you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Mara's Announcement and the Myrobalan Cure
title.zh: 魔王報死訊與訶子療疾

region.en: Bank of the Nairanjana (symbolic pin at Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 尼連禪河畔（以菩提伽耶為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: The honeyed food gives the Buddha colic, and Mara comes to announce that the time to die has come; but he answers that as long as his disciples have not become wise and of quick understanding, as long as the bhikshus, bhikshunis and lay disciples cannot refute their adversaries according to the Dharma, and as long as his moral teaching has not spread far and wide among gods and men, so long will he not pass away. Shakra brings an arura (myrobalan) fruit from Jambudvipa, and by it the Buddha is cured.
summary.zh: 蜜食令佛腹痛；魔王乘機來報「世尊，死期已至！」佛答：只要我的弟子尚未智慧猛利、四眾尚不能依正法折服論敵、正法尚未廣布天人世間——「我終不取滅度。」帝釋自閻浮提取一顆訶子（arura）來，佛因之而癒。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The Buddha sat down on the bank of the Nairanjana and ate the food which the merchants had given him, but the honey gave him colic. Then the Evil one, seeing the pain he was enduring, came to him and said, Blessed One, the time to die has come! But he answered him, Mara, as long as my disciples have not become wise and of quick understanding, as long as the bhikshus, the bhikshunis and the lay disciples of either sex are not able to refute their adversaries according to the Dharma, as long as my moral teaching has not been spread far and wide among gods and men, so long will I not pass away. Then Shakra brought an arura fruit from a tree in Jambudvipa, and by it the Buddha was cured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.

region.en: Abode of the Naga king Mutchilinda (symbolic pin near Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 目支鄰陀龍宮（以菩提伽耶附近為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Dulva (Kangyur Vinaya), translated c. 8th-9th century; Rockhill translation 1884

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884), ch. II

summary.en: After remaining under the Bo tree as long as pleased him, the Buddha went to where lived the Naga king Mutchilinda; wishing to protect him from the sun and rain, the serpent wrapped his body seven times around the Blessed One and spread out his hood over his head, and there the Lord remained seven days in thought.
summary.zh: 佛在菩提樹下隨意經行後，來到目支鄰陀龍王之處；龍王為其遮日避雨，以身繞佛七匝，展開傘蓋覆其頭頂——世尊在此思維七日。

sensitivity.note: Canonical narrative; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The Buddha went to where lived the Naga king Mutchilinda; and he, wishing to protect him from the sun and rain, wrapped his body seven times around the Blessed One, and spread out his hood over his head, and there the Lord remained seven days in thought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Life of the Buddha (1884); not verbatim.
